name: The Ferment Underground — Gray-Market Supper Club
creator: Collective (founding member: Orisanmi Kwak-Delacroix)
description: Operating since 2196 in rotating locations across Tier 2 and Tier 3 spaces — back rooms of licensed establishments, decommissioned water-treatment sub-floors, rented parking infrastructure — The Ferment Underground is GLMZ's longest-running underground supper club, organized around a single principle: every dish must contain at least one ingredient that is real, not synthesized. The collective sources through a gray-market supply chain connecting vertical farm workers, Great Lakes fishing cooperatives, and a small network of indoor soil farmers operating in technical violation of Axiom land-use codes. Dinners seat 30-60 people, cost Φ180-400 per head depending on ingredient availability, and are announced via encrypted neural-feed invitation 48 hours in advance.
cultural_impact: The Ferment Underground is credited with catalyzing the Real Ingredient Movement of the 2210s, which pushed for reclassification of genuine agricultural products as essential goods rather than luxury items. Its rotating membership has included food scientists, black-market horticulturalists, and at least two Axiom food-regulation inspectors.
controversy: In 2213, a Ferment Underground dinner was raided by Axiom food-safety enforcement; the charges (unlicensed real-protein service, unregistered fermentation, indoor soil farming within city limits) were ultimately dropped, but the founding collective member Orisanmi Kwak-Delacroix spent 40 days in administrative detention. The incident became the basis for the 'Thornfield food hearings' sidebar.
story_hooks: A new guest at a Ferment Underground dinner is clearly not who they claimed to be on their application — but their knowledge of pre-Synthesis fermentation technique is so specific that the collective is divided on whether to trust them.

The gray-market supply chain has been compromised: a vertical farm worker who was a key source has gone silent, and the last three shipments contained trace geneware markers suggesting corporate interference.

Someone is publishing detailed accounts of Ferment Underground dinners to an open neural feed — accurate enough to only come from an insider — and the collective must decide how to find them before enforcement does.
